blocks.text: 4 - 1 Basic Definitions and Concepts
The basic concepts related to the circle. The concept of axis of symmetry in the circle.
Key term: Circle
Key term: Surface of a circle
Key term: Radius
Key term: chord
Key term: Diameter
Key term: Axis of symmetry in a circle
Yousef used the program, Google Earth, on his computer to study the geography of Egypt. Yousef noticed some green, circular areas next to the desert areas so, he asked his father about them.

The father Said: You learn that a drop of water means the source of life. Therefore, we should minimize the consumption of water in order to irrigate the land by the central irrigation method (sprinkle irrigation) in which, the wheels of the irrigation machine circle around a fixex point which draws those circles.
The circle is the set of points of a plane which are at constant distance from a fixed point in the same plane.
The fixed point is called the centre of the circle and the constant distance is called the radius length.
A circle is usually denoted by its center: circle M means the circle whose center is point M.
When drawing circle M in a plane, it divides the points of the plane in to three sets of points as in the figure, and they are :
The set of points inside the circle, like points M, D, E, ...
The set of points on the circle, like points A, B, C, ...
The set of points outside the circle, like points X, Y, Z, ...
Surface of the circle: the set of points of the circle ∪ the set of points inside the circle. $\text{circle} \cup \text{interior points}$
Radius of a circle: a line segment with one endpoint at the center and the other endpoint on the circle.
In the figure opposite $\overline{MA}$, $\overline{MB}$, $\overline{MC}$ are radii for circle M where: MA = MB = MC = radius length of the circle (r)
Two circles are congruent if their radii are equal in length.
The chord: a line segment whose end points are any two points on the circle.
Diameter: the chord passing through the center of the circle.
Symmetry in the circle
From the previous activity we deduce that :
Any straight line passing through the center of a circle is an axis of symmetry of it.
Important Corollaries
From 1: the straight line passing through the center of the circle and the midpoint of any chord of it is perpendicular to this chord.
From 2: the straight line passing through the center of a circle and perpendicular to any chord of it bisects this chord.
From 3: the perpendicular bisector of any chord of a circle passes through the center of the circle.

lessons.title: Positions of a point, a Straight Line and a Circle with Respect to a Circle

blocks.text: What you'll learn: Identifying the position of a point with respect to a circle. Position of a straight line with respect to a circle. Relation of the tangent with the radius of a circle. Position of a circle with respect to another circle. Relation of the line of centers with the common chord and the common tangent.
Key term: Point is outside a circle.
Key term: Point is on the circle
Key term: Point is inside a circle.
Key term: Two distant circles.
Key term: Two intersecting circle.
Key term: Two circles touching
Key term: Common tangent
Key term: Line of centers
Key term: Common chord
First: Position of a point with respect to a circle.
In the figure opposite, circle M divides the points of the plane in to three sets of points.
If M circle with radius length r and A was a point on the circle plane, then:
If A is outside the circle, then MA > r, and vice versa. $MA > r$
If A is on the circle, then MA = r, and vice versa. $MA = r$
If A is inside the circle, then MA < r, and vice versa. $MA < r$
Second: Position of a straight line with respect to a circle :
If M circle with radius length of r, L is a straight line on its plane, $\overleftrightarrow{MA} \perp L$ where $\overleftrightarrow{MA} \cap L = \{A\}$, Then:
The straight line L is located outside the circle M, L ∩ circle M = ϕ; so MA > r and vice versa. $L \cap M = \phi,\ MA > r$
The straight line L is a secant to the circle M, L ∩ circle M = {C, D}; so MA < r and vice versa. $L \cap M = \{C, D\},\ MA < r$
The straight line L is tangent to circle M, L ∩ the circle = {A}; so MA = r and vice versa. $L \cap M = \{A\},\ MA = r$
Important facts
A tangent to a circle is perpendicular to the radius at its point of tangency.
If a straight line is perpendicular to a diameter of a circle at one of its endpoints, then it is a tangent to the circle.
Third: Position of a circle with respect to another circle.
The straight line l = line MN is called the line of centers of the two circles M and N, and it is an axis of symmetry for both of them.
Point 4: If $MN = r_1 - r_2$, then $M \cap N = \ldots$ (blank), surface of circle M ∩ surface of circle N = ... (blank), and the two circles are touching internally. $MN = r_1 - r_2$

Point 5: If $MN < r_1 - r_2$, then $M \cap N = \ldots$ (blank), surface of circle M ∩ surface of circle N = ... (blank), and the two circles are intersecting as in figure ... (blank). $MN < r_1 - r_2$
When $MN = 0$ (zero), the two circles are concentric, as in figure ... (blank). $MN = 0$
Corollaries
The line of centers of two touching circles passes through a point of tangency and is perpendicular to the common tangent.
The line of centers of two intersecting circles is perpendicular to the common chord and bisects it.
Notice that:
If ABC is a right-angled triangle at A and AD ⊥ BC, then (AB)² = BD × BC (Euclidean theorem). $(AB)^2 = BD \times BC$
Also (AD)² = DB × DC (Corollary). $(AD)^2 = DB \times DC$
Also AD × BC = AB × AC. $AD \times BC = AB \times AC$

blocks.text: 4-3 Identifying the circle
What you'll learn: How to draw a circle passing through a given point. How to draw a circle passing through two given points. How to draw a circle passing through three given points.
Key term: Circumcircle
A circle can be drawn (identified) with given terms:
A circle can be drawn (identified) with given terms: 1. the center of the circle.
A circle can be drawn (identified) with given terms: 2. the radius length of the circle.
First: Drawing a circle passing through a given point :
Given: A is a given point on the plane. R.T.P: Draw a circle passing through point A. Construction:
Construction step 1: take any chosen point as M on the same plane.
Construction step 2: place the tip of the compass at M and with an opening equal to MA draw the circle M. The circle M passes through point A.
Construction step 3: place the tip of the compass at another point M₁ and with an opening equal to M₁A draw circle M₁. The circle M₁ passes through point A.
Construction step 4: repeat the previous work and note the following.
For each chosen point (center of the circle) it is possible to draw a circle passing through point A.
From the previous we deduce that:
An infinite number of circles can be drawn passing through a given point such as A.
If the radii of these circles are equal in length, then their centers are located on a congruent circle whose center is point A.
Second: Drawing a circle passing through two given points:
Given: A and B are two given points in the plane. R.T.P: Draw circle M passing through the two points A and B i.e AB is a chord in circle M.
Construction:
Draw the straight segment AB.
Draw the straight line L, the axis of AB, where L ∩ AB = {F} (the center of the circle is on the axis of the chord AB).
Take any chosen point M where M ∈ L, put the tip of the compass at M and with an opening equal to MA draw circle M; it passes through point B.
Put the tip of the compass at another point M1 where M1 ∈ L, and with an opening equal to M1A draw circle M1; it passes through point B.
Repeat the previous work and note:
For each chosen point E on the axis of AB (center of the circle), it is possible to draw a circle passing through the two points A and B.
From the previous, we deduce that :
An infinite number of circles can be drawn to pass through two given points like A and B.
The radius of the smallest circle that can be drawn to pass through the two points A and B equals half the length of AB. $\frac{1}{2}\overline{AB}$
Two circles cannot intersect in more than two points.
Third : Drawing a circle passing through three given points:
Given: A, B and C are three given points on the plane. R.T.P: Draw circle M passing through the three points A, B and C.
Construction:
Draw the straight line $L_1$, the axis of $\overline{AB}$, thus $M \in L_1$. $M \in L_1$
Draw the straight line $L_2$, the axis of $\overline{BC}$, thus $M \in L_2$. $M \in L_2$
If $L_1 \cap L_2 = \{M\}$, place the tip of the compass at point M with an opening equalling MA. Draw the circle M. You will find it passing through the two points B and C. $L_1 \cap L_2 = \{M\}$
If A, B and C are collinear then $L_1 \parallel L_2$ and $L_1 \cap L_2 = \phi$. $L_1 \parallel L_2, L_1 \cap L_2 = \phi$
A circle cannot be drawn passing through the three points A, B and C (when collinear).
From the previous, we deduce that :
There is one and only one circle which passes through three noncollinear points.
Corollaries
The circle which passes through the vertices of a triangle is called the circumcircle of this triangle.
A triangle is said to be inscribed in a circle if its vertices are on the circle.
The perpendicular bisectors of the sides of a triangle intersect at a point which is the center of the circumcircle of the triangle.

lessons.title: The Relation Between the Chords of a Circle and its Center

blocks.text: The relation between the chords of a circle and its center
Deducing the relation between the chords of a circle and its center. How to solve problems related to the relation between the chords of a circle and its center.
Key term: Equal chords
Key term: Congruent circles
In the figure opposite: A is a point on circle M the chords AB, AC, AD, AE, AF were inscribed in it.
Notice that: The distance of chord AE from the center of circle M equals MX where X is the midpoint of the chord AE, in circle M which its radius length is r.
(MX)^2 + (AX)^2 = (AM)^2 = r^2, a constant expression. $(MX)^2+(AX)^2=(AM)^2=r^2$
The closer the chord is from the center of the circle, the longer its length is and vice versa.
Theorem: If chords of a circle are equal in length, then they are equidistant from the center.
Given: $AB = CD$, $\overline{MX} \perp \overline{AB}$, $\overline{MY} \perp \overline{CD}$. R.T.P.: Prove that $MX = MY$. Construction: Draw $\overline{MA}$, $\overline{MC}$.

Proof: ∵ $\overline{MX}\perp\overline{AB}$ ∴ $AX=\frac{1}{2}AB$. ∵ $\overline{MY}\perp\overline{CD}$ ∴ $CY=\frac{1}{2}CD$. ∵ $AB=CD$ ∴ $AX=CY$. ∵ the two triangles AXM and CYM both have: $AM=CM$; $m(\angle AXM)=m(\angle CYM)=90^\circ$; $AX=CY$ (Proof). ∴ $\triangle AXM \equiv \triangle CYM$. We get: $MX=MY$ (Q.E.D.)
Corollary: In congruent circles, chords which are equal in length are equidistant from the centers.
In the figure opposite: The two circles M and N are congruent, $AB = CD$, $\overline{MX}\perp\overline{AB}$, $\overline{NY}\perp\overline{CD}$, then: $MX = NY$.
Converse of the theorem: In the same circle (or in congruent circles) chords which are equidistant from the center(s) are equal in length.

If $m(\angle ABE) = m(\angle AEB)$, then prove that: $CD = ZL$.

steps.text: Proof: In $\triangle ABC$: $\because m(\angle ABE) = m(\angle AEB)$ $\therefore AB = AE$.
In the larger circle: $AB = AE$ (proof) $\therefore MX = MY$ (theorem)
